history.alt_text: Two official regulatory rate documents layered slightly out of alignment on a plain desk.
history.caption: A last-mile carbon score is often determined by the choice of a published rate factor rather than a real change on the road.
history.title: carbon-factor-rate-table-flatlay

style_when: the story is regulatory or contractual — a filing, a mandate, a rate notice, a certificate, a purchase order that changed the economics
prompt: Overhead flat-lay photograph of paper documents on a plain matte desk surface, shot with a 50mm overhead flat-lay optic with a razor-sharp focal plane. Top-down 90-degree view, asymmetric composition with generous editorial negative space on the right. Two thick, official regulatory rate documents and clipped filings layered slightly out of alignment to look handled, sitting on a textured grey desk. Even diffused daylight casting soft contact shadows, muted tactile paper tones, blank or illegibly cropped paper, creating a quiet, refined editorial aesthetic.
negative_prompt: text, letters, numbers, wordmarks, signage, UI, watermarks, logos
rationale: The story revolves around administrative rates, published factors, and the discrepancy between official regulatory documents. A document flatlay perfectly captures the bureaucratic reality of calculating carbon scores.
subject: two official regulatory rate documents layered slightly out of alignment
core_thesis: A last-mile carbon score is calculated using published rate factors that vary between agencies, rather than absolute physical emissions.
core_conflict: Variable published administrative rates vs absolute physical carbon reporting
alt_text: Last-Mile Carbon Rates. Two official regulatory rate documents layered slightly out of alignment on a plain desk.
caption: Last-Mile Carbon Rates: Why your fleet's carbon score is just a published rate.
title: Last-Mile Carbon Rates
